report:
## Conclusion

Yes—modest but real benefit. The best current evidence (a 2023 Cochrane systematic review update of 50 trials and a 2017 meta-analysis in the Journal of Nutrition) indicates that regular intake of cranberry juice or cranberry proanthocyanidin (PAC) extracts modestly reduces the risk of recurrent urinary tract infections (UTIs) in women prone to them, without major safety concerns. The Cochrane review found roughly a 6-percentage-point absolute reduction in recurrence (about 18% vs 24% with placebo), a relative risk reduction of roughly 25%, with the clearest benefit in women with recurrent UTIs, children, and people susceptible after urologic procedures—though evidence quality is limited by small trial sizes, high dropout rates, and heterogeneity in product formulation and dosing (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7027998/; jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2804706). The 2017 meta-analysis of otherwise healthy women similarly concluded cranberry lowers recurrent UTI risk by about 26% and can be a reasonable nonpharmacologic preventive option (pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29046404/). Notably, effectiveness appears dose-dependent on proanthocyanidin content: randomized trials comparing high- versus low-dose standardized PAC extracts found that higher PAC doses (≥36 mg/day) more effectively reduced recurrence and pyuria episodes than lower doses (link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12894-021-00811-w).

Overall, cranberry products—particularly standardized, higher-PAC extracts—appear to offer a modest, generally safe reduction in recurrent cystitis risk in women, though they are not as effective as antibiotic prophylaxis and results vary by product quality and adherence. They may be considered as an adjunct or alternative preventive strategy, especially for women wishing to avoid antibiotics, but expectations should be tempered given inconsistent trial quality and modest effect sizes.
